title: Electrically Reconfigurable Silicon Carbide Nanophotonic Cavities on Thin-Film Lithium Niobate
authors: San Lam Ng, Georgii Grechko, Vladislav Bushmakin, Rainer Stöhr, Vadim Vorobyov, Roman Kolesov, Jörg Wrachtrup
abstract: Interfacing integrated photonics with solid-state spin defects holds great promise for future quantum networks, but the scaling of spin-photon architectures is hindered by frequency mismatches arising from fabrication-induced variations in photonic cavity resonances and the inhomogeneous optical transition frequencies of individual spins. These challenges call for a photonic platform with deterministic and wide-range tunability. Here, we demonstrate a hybrid nanophotonic platform based on direct bonding of silicon carbide photonic crystal nanocavity arrays onto thin-film lithium niobate on insulator, enabling deterministic electrical tuning of multiple SiC nanocavities into mutual spectral resonance. By exploiting the strong electro-optic response of lithium niobate, we achieve continuous and wide-range cavity tuning of 380 GHz ($\sim$1.1 nm), sufficient to compensate both cavity disorder and spin inhomogeneity. The nanocavities balance strong optical confinement with electrical tunability, exhibiting a theoretical Purcell factor of approximately 400. This hybrid platform enables electrically reconfigurable spin-photon interfaces for large-scale integrated quantum photonics.
summary: The authors report on a novel hybrid nanophotonic platform combining SiC nanocavities, which host spin defects, with thin-film Lithium Niobate. By exploiting the strong electro-optic effect of LNOI, they achieved wide-range electrical tuning ($\sim 380 	ext{ GHz}$) for multiple cavities. This breakthrough overcomes frequency mismatch issues, creating a robust and scalable platform for integrated quantum photonics and spin-photon interactions.
main_problem: Scaling spin-photon architectures is hindered by frequency mismatches arising from fabrication variations in photonic cavity resonances and inhomogeneous optical transition frequencies of individual spins.
main_result: The hybrid platform successfully demonstrates deterministic electrical tuning of multiple SiC nanocavities into mutual spectral resonance, enabling scalable quantum photonic interfaces.
method: A 'break and bond' process was used to integrate SiC photonic crystal arrays onto thin-film Lithium Niobate on Insulator (TFLN), allowing for external voltage application to tune the cavities electro-optically.
model_or_system: The system is a hybrid nanophotonic platform combining Silicon Carbide (SiC) photonic crystal nanocavity arrays, which host spin defects (like V2 centers), with TFLN. The strong electro-optic response of TFLN provides the necessary wide-range tunability.
key_observables: Electrical tuning range ($\sim 380 	ext{ GHz}$ or $1.1 	ext{ nm}$), Purcell factor (theoretical $\approx 400$), readout/initialization fidelities ($>94\%$).
important_parameters: TFLN thickness, electro-optic coefficient of TFLN, cavity Q factors ($\sim 6 	imes 10^3$ to $13 	imes 10^3$).
main_assumptions: The weak electro-optic response of SiC necessitates the use of a high-electro-optic material like TFLN for tuning.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate cavity design schematics, the three-step fabrication process (SiC etching, bonding to LNOI, electrode deposition), and experimental results confirming electrical resonance shifts across multiple cavities.
paper_structure: The paper details the necessity of tunable platforms for spin-photon interfaces, describes the hybrid SiC/TFLN platform construction via direct bonding, presents characterization showing wide-range electrical tuning, and concludes by demonstrating high fidelity quantum operations potential.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses a major engineering bottleneck in solid-state quantum networking—frequency mismatch—by integrating two disparate physical systems (semiconductor photonics and electro-optic materials) to achieve deterministic tunability for coupling qubits to photons.

figures.caption: Figure 1: a. Schematic illustration of the cavity design. b. Simulation of the cavity bandgap, both resonance modes are placed at the middle of the bandgap. c. Simulation of the in-plane component of a unit cell. d. Simulation of the in-plane component of the resonance modes. The left figures show the top view, with dash line indicating the position of cavity centre. The right figures show the cross section view at the positions of field maxima. e. Simulated dependence of tuning sensitivity and mode volume on thin film LN thickness, showing that either the mode volume or the tuning sensitivity could be optimized depending on the need.

Figure 2: Outline of the fabrication procedure. The fabrication process is loosely divided into three parts. 1. Fabrication of triangular corrugated cavities from 4H-SiC by e-beam lithography followed by e-beam metal evaporation and reactive ion etching. 2. Bonding of nanobeams to LNOI by direct bonding. 3. Electrode fabrication and protective cladding of cavities.

Figure 3: Images of bonded cavities. a. Optical image of a large matrix of bonded cavities of a high yield sample, demonstrating the efficiency of the bonding method. b. SEM image of an array of bonded cavities. c. Defect and taper sections of one of the cavity.

Figure 4: Results of electrical tuning tests. a. Laser scattering intensity as a function of frequency detuning for the TM mode of the cavity. Voltages were applied to the cavity in steps, and shifts in the resonance frequency were observed, verifying the successful tuning of cavity resonance. b,c. Voltage sweep performed on TE and TM mode of the cavity, confirming a tuning range of 380.8 GHz for TE and 49.1 GHz for TM mode. d,e. Tuning sensitivity (GHz V−1) of TE and TM modes of characterized cavities, the shaded region highlight the common spectral range among the tested cavities.

Figure 5: Estimated cavity enhancement for V2 centres under optimal placement. a. Solid arrows denote radiative transitions and dashed arrows denote non-radiative decay channel. b. Illustration of linewidth broadening of the two electron spin state selective transitions. Blue (orange) curve represents A2 (A1) transition and the green shade represents the spectral width of the resonance mode. The cavity mode is in resonance with the A2 transition. Spintronics.note: The paper describes a hybrid platform combining SiC nanocavities hosting spin defects with TFLN, which directly relates to the central theme of cavity QED in engineered spin-photon systems.
